response.internal_assessment: The RoboRide price cut to $0.12/mile with residential coverage is the single most threatening piece of news I have received since this started. This is not a marginal price adjustment — at $0.12/mile with 8-minute waits, car ownership stops making financial sense for a significant portion of Millfield residents. Fewer cars means fewer cars to wash. My job is not being eliminated by a robot replacing me at the car wash — it's being eliminated by people not buying the thing I service. That is a slower death but it's the same outcome. My runway is 1.6 months and my only buffer is $263/month surplus plus whatever gig income I can pull. The bike delivery income I was running on weekends is now under direct pressure too — RoboRide's delivery partnership means they are entering that exact space. I need to find a replacement income stream fast. The cert program is the real asset here. Four months in, I am probably at 25% completion. I need to stay enrolled, and I need to accelerate the EV pathway question with Carlos because the timeline on my current job is now shorter than I thought. The community center retraining grants are worth pursuing this month — even partial coverage of cert costs or a stipend would extend my runway meaningfully. Financial situation: savings $3,317, monthly essentials $1,200, spending index at 42 means everything is tight.

The auto sector revenue index at 79 confirms what I can see — fewer cars being sold and serviced means less car washing demand. People using robotaxis regularly (7%) is early but that adoption curve is not going backward. The spending index at 42 means my gig delivery income option is also getting squeezed — people spending less equals fewer food delivery orders. The RoboRide delivery partnership announcement is the direct threat to my bike gig income. I need to acknowledge that income source may not hold and find a replacement or intensify the cert-to-employment pathway.

chosen_actions.description: Continue automotive service technician certificate program at Millfield Community College without missing a single session. This is month four of eight — I am roughly at 25% completion. This month's priority is not just attendance: I need to pin down, definitively, whether EV modules exist in this curriculum and when they appear. I flagged this at tick 6, flagged it again at tick 7, and still have not gotten the answer. This month I walk up to the program coordinator after Thursday's class and ask the question directly. I also want to know if there is an EV specialization add-on or follow-on credential the college offers, and what the timeline looks like. The general automotive cert is still worth finishing — it is the foundation — but I need to know if I am building toward the right second credential so I can plan the 8 months after this program ends.

resources.detail: 32 hours of evening and weekend classes across the month, no financial cost this tick as tuition was prepaid

chosen_actions.reasoning: The cert program is the single most important asset I am building. Four months in, unbroken streak. The EV curriculum question is overdue — at this displacement acceleration rate, graduating with the wrong credential in four months would be worse than not graduating at all. I need to know what I am graduating into.

chosen_actions.description: Have a direct conversation with Carlos (mechanic_carlos) — not a casual check-in but a focused ask: given that RoboRide just cut prices and expanded to residential, and given that Carlos is doing EV certification himself, what does he think the realistic timeline is for the Millfield general automotive sector? How long does he think the car wash has? And is the MCC general automotive cert a viable foundation for the EV specialization path he is on, or am I building the wrong thing? I am not asking him to hire me and I am not asking him for reassurance. I am asking him to give me his honest read on the market timeline because his information quality is higher than mine and I trust him enough to use that information. Five to ten minutes. No ask, just intelligence gathering.

resources.detail: Drawing on trust relationship (0.78) to get honest market read; giving attention and respect in return

chosen_actions.reasoning: Carlos has watched the auto sector for years and is himself navigating the EV transition. His trust score is 0.78 — high enough to ask the unvarnished question. The RoboRide residential expansion is a visible acceleration event and I want his read on it before I make any decisions about whether to stay in the cert program as-is or change course.

chosen_actions.description: Visit Kevin O'Brien's community center office hours this month to ask about retraining grants or stipends that could apply to my MCC automotive certificate program. I have been carrying a thin 1.6-month runway for multiple ticks and it has not improved enough. If there is a grant that offsets even partial tuition or provides a monthly stipend for workers actively retraining, that directly extends my financial runway without requiring me to take on more work hours. I will bring documentation: enrollment verification from MCC, my current employment status at the car wash, income level. This is not charity — this is me doing what a functioning support system is supposed to enable. The ask is low-ego. If there is money available, I want it. If there is not, I will know for certain and stop hoping it might appear.

resources.detail: Potential monthly retraining stipend or grant offset; estimated $150/month if approved, could significantly improve 1.6-month runway

chosen_actions.reasoning: My runway is the constraint. The cert program costs time and some money. If there is institutional support available for exactly this situation — low-wage worker, active retraining, sector under displacement pressure — then this is precisely the tick to access it. Employment rate at 73%, spending index at 42, RoboRide expanding: this is the kind of environment those programs were designed for.

chosen_actions.description: Do not change jobs this tick, do not quit the car wash, do not take on a new gig income stream to replace bike delivery. The bike delivery income is now under pressure from RoboRide's delivery partnership but replacing it would require time hours I need for the cert program. The car wash job is more precarious than before but I still have it and the income is real. The rational play is to hold my current income sources, protect my class schedule, pursue the grant, and let Carlos's intelligence inform whether I accelerate any credential decisions. Acting impulsively to replace the gig income this tick would cost class time and the cert is worth more than the $100/month the gig was generating.

resources.detail: Deliberate choice not to scramble for replacement gig income this tick

chosen_actions.reasoning: RoboRide's delivery partnership makes bike delivery gig income less viable going forward. But replacing it now would mean either sacrificing class hours (bad) or adding an unsustainable schedule (also bad). The $100/month was a buffer, not a foundation. Losing it hurts the runway but not fatally — savings are $3,317 and I have a real income source in the cert program destination. The grant search is a better use of that energy.

response.inner_monologue: RoboRide just made my job category smaller and my gig income stream more competitive at the same time, in one announcement. I see it. I am not pretending it is fine. But I have been building toward a different future for four months and I am not stopping now — I am going to class, I am going to ask the EV question I have been circling, I am going to sit down with Kevin O'Brien and ask if there is money available for someone doing exactly what I am doing. The economy is contracting around me but I am still the one person in my circle who enrolled in a cert program before the floor fell out. That gap is everything.
